text:
Hundreds of millions of people still lack a safe and reliable water supply. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on clean water access: better health and wider opportunities for education and work.

First and foremost, clean water protects health. Safe drinking water prevents diseases such as diarrhoea and cholera, which kill many young children, and proper sanitation stops infections from spreading. As a result, fewer people become ill, hospitals are less crowded and families spend less on medicine. A village that gains a safe tap, for example, sees fewer children miss school because of stomach illness, and healthier adults are able to work more regularly. In the long term, a healthy population is also cheaper for the country to support.

In addition, clean water frees time for education and work. Where there is no tap nearby, women and girls often spend several hours every day carrying water, which stops them from attending school or earning money. Piped water removes this burden, so more girls can complete their education and more adults can take paid jobs. Reliable water also supports farming, food processing and manufacturing, which raises productivity and attracts investment. Healthier, better-educated people make the economy stronger, and the benefits continue across generations. Clean water is therefore an investment in people rather than simply a public service. Although building pipes and treatment plants requires large investment, studies in many countries suggest that the returns in health and productivity are far greater than the cost.

To sum up, clean water access brings clear benefits to a country, above all better health and wider opportunities. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.
